section.title: The New Life in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Having freed the Colossians from human regulations, Paul now shows the true shape of Christian living, grounded not in rules but in union with the risen Christ. Because they have died and been raised with Christ and their life is hidden with Him in God, they are to seek the things above, put to death the old self, and put on the new self, clothing themselves in Christlike virtues, with love binding all together and the peace and word of Christ ruling their common life. This is the positive answer to legalism: real transformation flowing from union with Christ.
section.thesis: Because believers have been raised with Christ and their life is hidden with Him in God, they are to set their minds above, put to death the old self and put on the new, clothing themselves in compassion, forgiveness, and love, letting the peace and word of Christ rule so that everything is done in His name with thanksgiving.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the foundation, raised with Christ and hidden with Him in God, set your minds above; putting off the old self, the vices of the earthly nature; and putting on the new self, Christlike virtues bound by love, with the peace and word of Christ ruling the community, all done in His name with thanks.

units.label: Raised with Christ
units.note: your life is hidden with Christ in God

verses.text: Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.
Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.
For you died, and your life is now {{krypto|hidden}} with Christ in God.
When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory.

units.label: Put off the old self
units.note: put to death the earthly nature

verses.text: Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry.
Because of these, the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
When you lived among them, you also used to walk in these ways.
But now you must put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips.
Do not lie to one another, since you have taken off the old self with its practices,

units.label: Put on the new self
units.note: clothed in virtue, bound by love, ruled by peace

verses.text: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the {{eikon|image}} of its Creator.
Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all.
Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.
Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.
And over all these virtues put on {{agape|love}}, which is the bond of perfect unity.
Let the {{eirene|peace}} of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful.
Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.

krypto.gloss: To hide, conceal, or keep safe. Paul says your life is now hidden with Christ in God, using a perfect tense that means it has been safely stored and remains so. The believer's true life is not on display or at risk in this world; it is kept secure with Christ and will be revealed in glory when He appears.

eikon.gloss: Image, likeness, a true representation. The new self is being renewed in the image of its Creator, restoring what was marred at the fall when humanity, made in God's image, turned away. Since Christ Himself is the image of the invisible God, 1:15, to be renewed in God's image is to be conformed to Christ.

agape.gloss: Self-giving love that seeks the good of others, the highest Christian virtue. Paul says to put love on over all the other virtues, for it is the bond that ties them together in perfect unity. Love is not one item on the list but the belt that holds the whole wardrobe of Christlike character in place.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, the settled well-being that comes from being reconciled to God. Paul tells the peace of Christ to rule, literally to act as umpire or referee, in their hearts and among them as one body. This peace, secured by the cross, is to govern the community's life and settle its disputes.

basic.context: After freeing the church from man-made rules, Paul shows what real Christian living looks like. It flows from union with the risen Christ. Because you died and rose with Him, and your true life is safely hidden with Him in God, aim your heart at the things above. Then get rid of the old ways, sexual sin, greed, anger, slander, and lies, and put on the new self, dressing in compassion, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, and above all love. Let Christ's peace and Christ's word govern your life together, and do everything in His name with thankfulness.
basic.hermeneutics: The whole ethic is grounded in indicative before imperative: because you have been raised with Christ, therefore live this way. Paul uses the picture of taking off dirty clothes and putting on clean ones to describe real, ongoing change. These commands are for all believers, and they are the true alternative to the empty rule-keeping of chapter two.
basic.originalLanguages: Your real life is krypto, hidden and kept safe, with Christ in God. The new self is renewed in the eikon, the image, of its Creator, which means being made like Christ, who is God's image. Over every virtue you are to put on agape, love, the bond that ties them together. And the eirene, the peace, of Christ is to rule, to act as umpire, in your hearts and your shared life.
basic.typology: Being renewed in the image of the Creator restores humanity made in God's image in Genesis, now reformed after Christ, the true image. The new community where there is no Jew or Greek, slave or free, fulfills God's promise to gather one people from all nations. Putting off and putting on echoes the priestly changing of garments, now applied to every believer.
basic.christ: Christ is the risen Lord seated at God's right hand, and He is our very life, so that when He appears we will appear with Him in glory. He is the image into which we are being remade. He is all and in all in the new community, and His forgiveness is the pattern for ours. His peace rules our hearts and His word dwells in us richly.
basic.god: God raised Christ and seats Him at His right hand, and it is with God that our life is hidden and safe. God is the Creator whose image is being restored in us, and the Father to whom we give thanks through Christ. He chooses a people, holy and beloved, and calls them into one reconciled body.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 4 gives the same picture of taking off the old self and putting on the new. Romans 6 grounds new life in dying and rising with Christ. And Galatians 3 declares that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free.
basic.oneStory: This is the renewal of humanity that the whole Bible anticipates: image-bearers, ruined at the fall, remade after Christ the true image, and gathered into one new people from every nation. The risen life of Christ now shapes a community marked by love, forgiveness, and peace, a preview of the glory to be revealed when He appears.

context.literary:
The passage turns on the little word "therefore" at 3:1 and then runs in three waves, each opening with a change of clothes. The first wave (verses 1 to 4) is built from two imperatives about the mind and two reasons: seek the things above, set your minds there, because you died and your life is hidden with Christ. The tenses matter. "You died" and "have been raised" point to a past event, "is hidden" is a perfect that stays in force, and "appears" looks forward to a future event. Past, present and future are all packed into the foundation before a single command about behavior is given.

The second wave (verses 5 to 11) is a vice list in two groups. Verse 5 names sins of the body and the wanting self (sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, greed) and verse 8 names sins of the mouth and the temper (anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy language, then lying). The first group is "put to death", the second is "put aside", and Paul breaks the rhythm in verse 9 with one short command, "Do not lie to one another," placed exactly where the list moves to the new self. Verses 10 and 11 widen the camera from the individual to the whole community: the new self is a corporate reality in which every dividing line is dissolved.

The third wave (verses 12 to 17) is a virtue list with a clear architecture. Five garments are named in verse 12, two actions toward each other in verse 13 (bear with, forgive), love over everything in verse 14, and then three rulers of the shared life: Christ's peace, Christ's word and Christ's name. The word thanks, in its different forms, closes verses 15, 16 and 17, so that the passage ends in a tide of gratitude. The shape is not a random list but a movement from the heart, to the community, to the whole of life.
context.historical:
The Colossian church was a small, mixed congregation in a provincial town, probably meeting in homes, 4:15, and made up largely of Gentiles who had once worshiped other gods, 1:21 and 2:13. When Paul says "you also used to walk in these ways" in verse 7, he is speaking to people whose old life included temple meals, household cults and the ordinary vices of a Greek city. The sins in verses 5 and 8 were not abstract. They were the accepted manners of the world these believers had left.

The list of social categories in verse 11 reflects the real tensions of the region. Jews and Greeks lived side by side in Phrygia, and Josephus describes Jewish communities established there for generations. Circumcised and uncircumcised named the religious line between them. "Barbarian" was the Greek label for anyone who did not speak Greek, and the Scythians, from the far north of the Black Sea, were the standard example of the savage outsider. Paul names the lowest rung of Greek contempt on purpose: even the Scythian is welcome. Slave and free described a gulf that organized the whole economy. Many of the Colossians, including Onesimus, named in 4:9 and called a slave in the background of the letter to Philemon, lived on one side or the other of that line.

Clothing is a vivid image in the ancient world, where garments displayed rank and role. Converts to some religions changed their dress when they entered a new community. Baptism in the early church often involved removing and then putting on clothing, though how early the practice was fixed is uncertain, and Paul's image does not depend on it. The picture of an old self removed and a new self put on would have been immediately understandable to people who knew that what one wore said who one was.
context.canonical:
The passage is a rereading of the opening of the Bible. The "image of its Creator" in verse 10 is the image of Genesis 1:26 and 27, and the whole direction of Scripture is to restore what was lost there. The vice lists are a portrait of the world after Genesis 3 and the cursing and murder of Genesis 4, while the virtues display what humanity was made to be. The phrase "chosen, holy and beloved" in verse 12 takes the three titles of Israel in Deuteronomy 7:6 to 8 and gives them to a church of Jews and Gentiles together. Peter does the same in 1 Peter 2:9.

The call to set the mind on things above has roots in the psalms of the enthroned king, since "Sit at My right hand" in Psalm 110:1 is the verse behind the picture of Christ seated in 3:1. The New Testament returns to that verse again and again. The command to forgive "as the Lord forgave you" sits on the great self-description of God in Exodus 34:6 as compassionate, gracious and slow to anger. The word of Christ dwelling richly recalls the Old Testament pattern of the law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, now fulfilled in the new covenant.

Elsewhere in Paul the same argument is built in other ways. Romans 6 and 8 give the death-to-life frame and the call to put to death the deeds of the body, Romans 8:13. Ephesians 4:22 to 24 and 5:3 to 6 repeat many of the same words almost directly, which shows that Colossians 3 reflects a stable piece of apostolic teaching and not a one-off remark. Galatians 3:27 and 28 uses clothing and the abolishing of social divisions in a very similar way.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants to answer the cheap charge that freedom from rules produces carelessness. He does so by relocating the source of holiness. Rules were an attempt to restrain the self from outside. He puts the power of change inside the believer's union with Christ: because you died with Him, the old self's claim is over; because you were raised with Him, you now live from above. The first hearers are meant to see that holiness is not an optional extra but the natural fruit of what has already happened to them.

He also wants the church to see that this is communal. The new self of verses 10 and 11 is a shared humanity, not a private improvement, and most of the virtues in verses 12 to 14 can only be practiced with other people, since they are acts of bearing, forgiving and teaching. The passage is aimed at a congregation where Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free had to share a table and a song. It shows them the resources, namely Christ's peace, word and name, by which that difficult fellowship can hold. The closing verse gathers the whole life under one test: can this be said or done in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks to the Father?
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 4 and 9 to 11 describe what is true of believers in Christ: you died, you were raised, you have taken off the old self and put on the new. Verses 5, 8, 12 to 17 prescribe what must follow: put to death, put aside, clothe yourselves, forgive, let peace rule. Paul's order is the key. The commands depend on the descriptions, so the call is never "become a new self by trying" but "be what you have been made."

Not every detail is a rule to be copied. The lists are examples and not complete catalogs. The vices stand for a pattern of life, and the virtues for the character of Christ, so a Christian who finds that a particular sin is not on the list has not been given a gap to live in. The pairs in verse 11 describe what the gospel does with human divisions; they are not a program for removing differences of language or office in the church, nor do they erase distinctions within marriage or ministry that other passages address. They state that none of these labels can separate anyone from Christ or from one another.

The commands to teach, admonish and sing apply directly to the church today. They also warn that a congregation's songs are a means of formation, not just a mood.

debates.question: Does 'you have taken off the old self' describe something finished at conversion, or something to be done daily?

views.label: A decisive past event
views.case: Verses 9 and 10 use aorist participles, 'having taken off' and 'having put on,' that describe an act completed at conversion and baptism. Romans 6:6 says the old self 'was crucified with Him', and Galatians 3:27 says that those baptized 'have clothed yourselves with Christ.' On this reading Paul states a fact, and the commands in verses 5 and 8 follow from it.

views.label: A daily practice
views.case: Parallel passages like Ephesians 4:22 and 24 use an infinitive, 'to put off' and 'to put on,' which can be read as a command, and 2 Corinthians 4:16 speaks of the inner self being 'renewed day by day.' The 'being renewed' of verse 10 is a continuing process, which suggests the old self has to be put off again each day.

views.label: Both, in different senses
views.case: Many combine the two. The change of identity happened once, but its implications have to be lived into. The participles state the position and the present participle 'being renewed' states the process, so the believer is told to become what he already is.

debates.bearing: The balance protects against two errors. If the old self is only a daily task, believers lose the assurance that the decisive change has been done for them; if it is only a past event, they may think no struggle is left. Verses 5 and 8 show that Paul expects both the standing and the struggle.

debates.question: Does 'no Greek or Jew, slave or free' abolish social distinctions or only their power to divide?

views.label: Distinctions end in Christ
views.case: Galatians 3:28 adds 'male nor female' and says all are one. Some argue that the gospel intends to erase these structures from the church's life, since the new humanity has no place for rank. They point to Philemon 1:16, where Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave.'

views.label: Distinctions remain, status is equalized
views.case: Others note that Paul continues to speak of husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and slaves in 3:18 to 4:1, so he does not think the categories vanish. The point is that none confers advantage before God or in the fellowship of the church. 1 Corinthians 7:17 to 24 keeps the categories while relativizing them.

views.label: A direction of travel
views.case: A third view reads the verse as the seed of a social change that works itself out over time. The gospel contains a principle that eventually dissolves slavery and ethnic hierarchy, even though Paul works within the structures of his age. Church history gives reasons to take this seriously and reasons for humility, since the principle was often long ignored.

debates.bearing: All three agree that in the body of Christ no one is a lesser member, and that Christ 'is all and is in all.' The passage leaves no room for ethnic or class pride in the church, and the immediate sequel in 3:22 to 4:1 shows how seriously Paul wants that principle lived.

study.originalLanguages:
The first command in verse 1 is zeteite, "seek" or "strive for," and verse 2 gives phroneite, "set your minds." Both are present imperatives, which describe a habit that has to be kept up. The second verb is richer than the English. Phroneo names the whole direction of thought and desire, the mindset that one carries, and Romans 8:5 and 6 uses it for the mind of the flesh against the mind of the Spirit. It is not a call to think only about heaven but to let the ruling Christ shape what the mind treats as important.

In verse 3 "you died" is aorist and "is hidden" is a perfect, kekryptai. The perfect says the hiding was done and stays done. Two cross-references show the meaning. The same verb family appears in 2:3, where all the treasures of wisdom are "hidden" in Christ. Paul is saying that the believer's life is kept where those treasures are kept, in Christ in God. The verse promises security, because what is hidden with Christ in God is out of reach of the powers, and it admits obscurity, since the world cannot see this life yet, verse 4.

Verse 5 says "Put to death," nekrosate, an aorist imperative, and the object is the melē, literally the "members" or limbs of the earthly nature. Paul is using a body image for habits: the sins are limbs of the old self which are to be killed, not reformed. Greed is pleonexia, the wanting of more, and the surprising line is that it "is idolatry." Ephesians 5:5 says the same. The point is that desire which treats a created good as ultimate has taken the place of God.

In verses 9 and 10 the participles are apekdysamenoi, "having taken off," and endysamenoi, "having put on." The first is the same verb Paul used in 2:15 for God stripping the powers and in 2:11 in its noun form for the putting off of the body of flesh. The second is the verb of dressing, used for the clothing of the new self again in verse 12, where the command is endysasthe. The new self is "being renewed," anakainoumenon, a present passive participle: God keeps renewing it, and the goal is epignosis, full knowledge, according to the image, kat' eikona, which is the Greek phrase of Genesis 1:27 in the Septuagint.

Verse 14 calls love the syndesmos, the "bond" that holds the virtues together, of teleiotes, "perfection" or completeness. The two words together can mean love is the bond that makes everything complete, or the bond which unites the community into a whole. The image is of a belt or a band that gathers loose garments. Ephesians 4:3 uses the same noun for the "bond of peace."

In verse 15 "rule" is brabeueto, to act as umpire, and it echoes the "disqualify" of 2:18. Paul has replaced the umpire. At the end of verse 15 and again in verses 16 and 17, thanks is repeated, eucharistoi and eucharistountes, so the sentence ends where the letter began in 1:12.

typology.fulfillment: Humanity was made to bear God's image and to represent Him. That image was marred in Adam and is restored in the new self, which is 'being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.' The correspondence runs through Christ, since He is 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15, and believers are being conformed to Him, Romans 8:29, and transformed from glory to glory, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The escalation is that the restored image is no longer only a created vocation but a share in the character of the Son. The type is still unfinished; 1 John 3:2 says we shall be like Him when He appears.

typology.type: The clothing of the priests and of Joshua, Exodus 29:5-9 and Zechariah 3:3-5
typology.fulfillment: The priests of Israel were given holy garments at their ordination, and Joshua the high priest, standing in filthy clothes, was stripped by command and clothed with splendid robes while the angel declared, 'I have removed your iniquity.' Paul's pattern of putting off and putting on echoes both. The correspondence is of a new role and a new identity given by God. In Christ every believer is clothed, Galatians 3:27, and the whole church is a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9. The type falls short in that the priests' garments covered a mediator for a time, while Christ is Himself the clothing of all His people.

typology.type: Israel as chosen, holy and beloved, Deuteronomy 7:6-8
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told that God had chosen them, set them apart as holy and set His love on them, though they were the smallest nation. Colossians 3:12 applies the same three titles to the church, which includes Gentiles. The correspondence is of election by grace and not merit. The escalation is that the people of God are no longer defined by one nation and one land but by union with Christ, Galatians 3:29. Where Israel failed under the covenant at Sinai, the church is given the Spirit and the word that dwells within, Jeremiah 31:33.

The psalm pictures the king seated at God's right hand until his enemies are made a footstool. Verse 1 of the chapter says that Christ is seated there now. The correspondence is of royal authority held by the Messiah. Believers share it in position, for Ephesians 2:6 says God 'seated us with Him in the heavenly realms,' and in hope, since they will 'appear with Him in glory.' The type falls short because the Davidic kings who first sat on the throne died, while this king lives and reigns forever, Hebrews 7:24.

typology.type: The people gathered from all nations, Isaiah 56:6-7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foretells foreigners who join themselves to the LORD and find welcome in a house of prayer for all the nations. Colossians 3:11 is the outcome: no Greek or Jew, barbarian or Scythian, because 'Christ is all and is in all.' The correspondence is of the nations brought into one worshiping people. Revelation 7:9 shows the final form, a multitude from every nation and tribe and tongue before the throne. The promise runs beyond this letter, since the gathering is not finished until the new creation.

study.christ:
The chapter begins with Christ seated, and everything else flows from His position. He is at the right hand of God, which is the place of rule, and He is the believer's life, verse 4. The phrase "Christ, who is your life" is among the strongest in the New Testament. Paul does not say that Christ gives life or shows the way to life. He says Christ is the life, so that the believer's existence is bound up with His as a branch with the vine. Where He is, they are, and when He appears they will appear with Him in glory.

The passage also presents Him as the pattern and the power for the new self. He is the image of God, 1:15, so being renewed in the image of the Creator means being renewed in the likeness of Christ. The virtues of verse 12 are the traits Philippians 2:5 to 8 describes in Him: compassion, humility, gentleness, patience. The forgiveness of verse 13 has a model and a measure, "Forgive as the Lord forgave you," and the Lord forgave at the cost of the cross, 2:13 and 14. Ephesians 4:32 gives the same standard. Christ is thus not only a moral example but the one whose act makes forgiveness possible and whose action sets its pattern.

He is Lord over the community. His peace is to rule the heart, verse 15; His word is to dwell richly among the people as they teach and sing, verse 16; and His name is the sign under which all words and deeds are done, verse 17. The "name" is not a magic formula but a statement of authority: to act in the name of the Lord Jesus is to act as His representative, under His approval. Since the Father receives thanks "through Him," He is also the mediator of worship.

Verse 11 gives the corporate Christ. "Christ is all and is in all" means that He is the only thing that finally matters about each person and that He dwells in each. The racial, religious and social labels fall away because He fills them. It would be a mistake to allegorize the clothes or the vices, as if each garment were a feature of Christ, but the general line is firm: the new humanity is made in Him, from Him and for Him.
study.god:
God is first of all the one who raises and exalts. The passage assumes that God raised Christ, seated Him at His right hand and raised believers with Him, which is the ground of verse 1. Everything else rests on a God whose power has already worked a change, since the hidden life is "with Christ in God," verse 3. The language of hiding speaks of a God who guards: He keeps what is His.

He is the Creator whose image is being restored in humanity, verse 10. This is not a new project but the original one: the Creator never abandoned His purpose for people made in His likeness. It shows a God who renews instead of discarding, which fits Genesis 1:27 and 2 Corinthians 5:17. The "knowledge" in which renewal happens implies a God who wants to be known, and who is the standard of human life, since the new self is shaped by what He is like.

He is a God of wrath and of mercy together. Verse 6 says that "the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience", so the vices in verse 5 are not minor matters. The same God has chosen, made holy and loved a people, verse 12, and forgave them in Christ, verse 13. The two statements are not in tension but depend on each other: the seriousness of the sin is what makes the forgiveness costly, and the forgiveness is what makes escape from the wrath possible. Passages like Exodus 34:6 and 7 hold the same pair together.

He is a God who makes one people from many. Verse 11 shows that He does not honor the divisions people treat as permanent, and verse 15 says believers were called "as members of one body." The Father is the one to whom the church directs its thanks through the Son, verse 17, and the song of the church is sung "to God," verse 16. This makes worship an overflow of what He has done and not a transaction.

For worship the passage shapes a clear rule. God is not honored by a split between private devotion and ordinary life, since "whatever you do, in word or deed" falls under His name. A God who is Lord of the whole of life is worshiped by a whole life, and the repeated thanks in these verses shows what attitude He asks for: not anxious striving, but gladness at what He has already given.

crossReferences.note: The closest parallel: put off the old self which is being corrupted by deceitful desires, be renewed in the spirit of your minds, put on the new self created to be like God. Reading it beside Colossians 3:9 and 10 shows the same teaching in two letters, and Ephesians adds that the new self is 'created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.'

Believers died with Christ and are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. This is the logic underneath Colossians 3:1 to 3. Romans adds the reason it is possible, that 'death no longer has dominion' over the risen Christ, and so none over those united to Him.

'Clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.' The image of laying aside deeds of darkness and putting on light matches Colossians 3:8 and 12. Paul seems to have a standard way of speaking about the Christian life as a change of clothes.

Those baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ, and the result is no Jew or Greek, slave or free. Colossians 3:10 and 11 run the same two ideas together: the new self put on, and the old divisions dissolved. Galatians shows that the clothing is Christ Himself.

Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Savior who will transform our bodies like His glorious body. It stands behind Colossians 3:1 to 4, the call to seek what is above and the promise of appearing with Him. The Philippians passage stresses the future transformation of the body.

'What we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him.' This is the same promise as Colossians 3:4, and John's phrase 'when Christ appears' uses the same verb. The hope of glory is a likeness to Christ that is hidden now and seen then.

The outer self wastes away while the inner self is renewed day by day. It supplies the daily side of Colossians 3:10, 'being renewed,' and shows that renewal is compatible with weakness and suffering, since it is the work of God in the inner person.

Those who live by the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit, and 'the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.' It explains why Paul puts the mind at the head of Colossians 3:2. A person's settled direction of thought is the decisive mark of whom he follows, and the result is life and peace, the same peace which rules in verse 15.

Sexual immorality, impurity and greed must not even be named among the saints, because no such person has an inheritance in the kingdom, and 'the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.' The wording of the final clause is identical to Colossians 3:6, so the two letters speak with one voice on why the vices matter.

Be filled with the Spirit, speak to one another with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, and give thanks always. It parallels Colossians 3:16 and 17 almost clause by clause, except that here the source is the Spirit and there it is the word of Christ, which shows the two are not rivals.

Israel is holy to the LORD, chosen and loved, not because it was large but because He set His affection on it. Colossians 3:12 gives these titles to the church, and the reason is the same: the love came first. The passage warns that the ground of holiness is grace and not achievement.

The LORD tells David's Lord to sit at His right hand until the enemies are made a footstool. Colossians 3:1 locates Christ there. The verse is the Old Testament anchor for the claim that the risen Jesus already reigns, and so the believer's life is joined to a throne.

By the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body and you will live. It sets beside Colossians 3:5 the means of the killing: the Spirit. Put to death is not self-effort but a work done in His power, which explains how Paul can command what he has also said is already done.

study.oneStory:
The passage answers a question that begins in Genesis: what became of the image of God in humanity? Genesis 1 makes people the Creator's likeness on the earth, and Genesis 3 and 4 show the likeness cracked by deceit, shame, envy and murder. Every vice in verses 5 and 8 can be traced to those chapters: lust and greed from the grasping at the fruit, anger and slander from Cain's rage, lying from the serpent's first words. The old self is Adam's way of being human, repeated.

Israel's story carried that problem forward. The law showed what a faithful people would look like and could not produce one. The prophets promised an answer in a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 11:19, and in a law written within, Jeremiah 31:33. Zechariah 3 pictured a defiled priest being stripped and re-clothed by God Himself. Colossians 3 announces that this promised exchange has happened, because the Messiah died and rose and His people have died and risen in Him.

The passage sits in the middle of redemption. The decisive act is behind it, in the cross and the empty tomb of the previous chapters, and the full result is still ahead, when Christ appears. The believers live in the stretch between, in a life already real but still hidden. That is why Paul sets a mind on things above beside a hard task on earth. They are told to live as people from the future, while the world still lives in the past.

What the chapter sets up is the household and the world mission of the chapters that follow. A people renewed in the image of the Creator will show a different pattern of marriage, parenting and work, 3:18 to 4:1, and will speak wisely to outsiders, 4:5 and 6.

The story ends in the new creation, where the image is fully restored. Believers will be like Him, 1 John 3:2. The dividing lines of Babel and of the old humanity are gone as a multitude from every nation and tribe stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The One on the throne says, "Behold, I make all things new," Revelation 21:5, and the new self of Colossians 3 is the first installment of that promise.

quiz.q: On what does Paul ground the call to seek the things above?

options.text: That believers have been raised with Christ and their life is hidden with Him in God.
options.note: Verses 1 to 3 root the new life in union with the risen Christ.

options.text: That believers must earn heaven by strict effort.
options.note: The command flows from grace already received, not from earning.

options.text: That earthly life has no value whatsoever.
options.note: Paul redirects the mind's focus; he does not despise all earthly life.

options.text: That believers should withdraw from the world entirely.
options.note: The passage calls for transformed living within the world, not withdrawal.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by putting to death the old self?

options.text: Actively renouncing sins like immorality, greed, anger, slander, and lying.
options.note: Verses 5 to 9 name concrete vices to put to death and put aside.

options.text: Feeling occasional regret without changing.
options.note: Paul calls for real removal of these sins, not mere regret.

options.text: Keeping a list of outward rules like chapter two.
options.note: This is not rule-keeping but Spirit-shaped transformation.

options.text: Withdrawing into harsh treatment of the body.
options.note: That asceticism was rejected in 2:23; here the change is inward and moral.

quiz.q: Into whose image is the new self being renewed?

options.text: The image of its Creator, that is, into the likeness of Christ.
options.note: Verse 10 ties renewal to the Creator's image, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: The image of the surrounding culture.
options.note: The pattern is God's image in Christ, not the culture.

options.text: The image of the false teachers' ideal.
options.note: Renewal is after the Creator, not any human ideal.

options.text: No particular image; it is undefined.
options.note: It is clearly the image of the Creator, restored in Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul say holds all the virtues together?

options.text: Love, which is the bond of perfect unity.
options.note: Verse 14 crowns the virtues with love as the binding garment.

options.text: Strict rule-keeping.
options.note: The binding virtue is love, not rules.

options.text: Personal ambition.
options.note: Ambition divides; love unites the body.

options.text: Fear of punishment.
options.note: It is love, not fear, that binds the virtues in unity.

quiz.q: What is to rule in the hearts and life of the church?

options.text: The peace of Christ, acting as umpire among members of one body.
options.note: Verse 15 lets Christ's peace govern the community's life.

options.text: Personal preference and majority opinion.
options.note: It is Christ's peace, not mere preference, that is to rule.

options.text: The demands of the false teachers.
options.note: Those demands were rejected; Christ's peace rules instead.

options.text: Constant competition for status.
options.note: Peace, not rivalry, is to govern the one body.

quiz.q: How does Paul say we should do everything, in word or deed?

options.text: In the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.
options.note: Verse 17 sums up the new life: all done in Christ's name with thanks.

options.text: For our own reputation and gain.
options.note: All is to be done in Jesus name, not for self-promotion.

options.text: Only when others are watching.
options.note: Sincerity toward the Lord, not performance, marks the new self.

options.text: According to whatever feels right in the moment.
options.note: The measure is the name of the Lord Jesus, not passing feelings.

questions: Your true life is hidden with Christ in God, safe and secure. How would resting in that security change the way you handle pressure and fear this week?
Paul calls you to set your mind on things above. What earthly things tend to capture your attention, and how could you deliberately lift your gaze to Christ?
Putting off the old self is active, not passive. Which specific sin is God calling you to put to death right now, and what would that look like in practice?
You are told to forgive as the Lord forgave you. Is there a complaint or grievance you are holding that Christ is calling you to release?
Everything is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus with thanks. How might naming Christ over your ordinary work and words reshape an average day?

translationNotes.note: Hidden renders a perfect tense, your life has been and remains safely stored with Christ in God, stressing security rather than concealment from view.
Some manuscripts read our life rather than your life; either way Christ Himself is named as the believer's life.
Rule translates a word for acting as umpire or arbiter; the peace of Christ is to decide and govern within the heart and the body.
